faq.q: Why does lactate increase in sepsis?

exam: A patient with fever, jaundice, and dark urine presents; what cellular process explains the jaundice and which bedside test helps differentiate malaria from hepatitis? — Explain haemolysis of infected erythrocytes and perform a malaria smear.

You see a hypotensive patient with warm extremities and a lactate of 4 mmol/L; what does this indicate about cellular metabolism and the next immediate management? — Recognise anaerobic metabolism; give oxygen, fluids, and treat underlying cause.

A child with severe malaria develops acute kidney injury; which cellular injury explains oliguria and what low‑resource intervention can limit damage? — Tubular cell necrosis; ensure adequate perfusion and avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
In a patient with septic shock, why is serum potassium often high, and how does this relate to cellular ion pumps? — Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase failure leads to K⁺ efflux; monitor and replace cautiously.

How does hypoxia‑inducible factor (HIF) alter cellular metabolism in high‑altitude patients, and what clinical sign might you observe? — Shifts to glycolysis; patient may have tachypnoea and mild metabolic acidosis.

A malnourished patient shows peripheral edema; differentiate between hypoalbuminemia‑related oncotic loss and endothelial leak due to infection. — Assess serum albumin, look for fever/inflammation, and examine for pitting edema.
Why is artesunate preferred over quinine for severe malaria in low‑resource settings? — Faster parasite clearance, lower cardiotoxicity, easier dosing.

A patient on high‑dose diuretics develops muscle weakness; which cellular electrolyte disturbance is responsible and how would you confirm it without lab tests? — Low potassium; confirm by clinical signs (cramps) and response to oral potassium.
ai.title: Cell Structure and Function
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The cell is the basic unit of life; understanding its components and how they interact guides diagnosis of many systemic diseases. Clinicians must link cellular dysfunction to bedside findings, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Plasma membrane: selective barrier, ion pumps, receptors
Cytoplasm: organelles for metabolism and protein synthesis
Nucleus: DNA storage, transcription control
sections.p: All human tissues are composed of cells that maintain homeostasis through membrane transport, energy production, and signalling. Recognising patterns of cellular injury helps explain organ failure.

b: Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase maintains resting membrane potential
Glucose transporters (GLUT1‑4) regulate cellular glucose uptake
Calcium signalling triggers muscle contraction and hormone release
sections.p: Energy (ATP) is generated mainly by mitochondria via oxidative phosphorylation; glycolysis provides rapid ATP when oxygen is limited. Transporters move nutrients, electrolytes, and waste across membranes.

b: Insulin‑mediated GLUT4 translocation in muscle and fat
Hypoxia‑inducible factor (HIF) up‑regulates glycolysis
Cortisol modulates protein catabolism
sections.p: Cellular activities are controlled by hormones, second messengers, and feedback loops. In low‑resource settings, malnutrition, infections, and toxins disrupt these pathways.

b: Ischemia → ATP depletion → loss of ion gradients → swelling
Oxidative stress → lipid peroxidation → membrane rupture
Infection‑induced apoptosis → organ dysfunction
sections.p: Cell injury can be reversible (e.g., hypoxia) or irreversible (necrosis, apoptosis). Common tropical causes include severe malaria, bacterial sepsis, and toxin exposure.

b: Acute kidney injury: tubular cell necrosis → oliguria
Septic shock: endothelial cell activation → capillary leak
Malaria severe anemia: parasite‑induced erythrocyte rupture
sections.p: Many bedside signs reflect cellular dysfunction: altered mental status (neuronal ATP loss), jaundice (hepatocyte bilirubin handling), and edema (endothelial leak). Understanding the cell guides targeted therapy.

t.b: Is tissue hypoxia present? – Elevated >2 mmol/L indicates anaerobic metabolism and predicts poor outcome.
Is malaria causing hemolysis? – Presence of parasites confirms diagnosis; if microscopy unavailable, rapid diagnostic test is acceptable.
Are ion pumps failing? – Abnormalities guide replacement and indicate cell membrane dysfunction.
Is glomerular filtration barrier damaged? – + protein suggests tubular or glomerular injury; if lab unavailable, assess for edema and hypertension.

b: Restore oxygen delivery: give supplemental O₂, treat anemia, correct hypotension.
Correct electrolyte disturbances: replace K⁺ cautiously, avoid rapid shifts.
Use antimalarials (artesunate) for severe malaria to stop parasite‑induced RBC lysis.
Provide glucose for hypoglycaemia to replenish ATP stores.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then support cellular metabolism and prevent further injury.

b: Septic shock vs. cardiogenic shock – both cause hypotension but have different cardiac findings.
Acute liver failure vs. severe malaria‑induced hemolysis – both cause jaundice; smear distinguishes.
sections.p: Cellular dysfunction can mimic organ‑specific disease.

b: Serum creatinine may stay normal despite early tubular injury; look for urine output changes.
Lactate can be falsely low if patient is hypovolaemic and sample delayed.
sections.p: Laboratory values may be normal early in injury.

b: Explain why lactate rises in shock.
Describe how malaria parasites destroy red cells at the cellular level.
Identify the bedside sign that reflects endothelial leak (pitting edema).
sections.p: Focus on linking cellular mechanisms to clinical presentation and resource‑limited investigations.
